how-to-organize-your-closet.body_html:
To organize your closet, take everything out, sort it into keep, maybe, donate, repair and out-of-season piles, group what stays by category, then store it so your most-worn pieces are the easiest to reach. Most of the work is deciding what earns a place, not buying containers. The steps below work for a walk-in, a small reach-in, or a closet you share.

Before you start: set a goal and block out the time

Decide what "organized" means for you. It might be faster mornings, more free space, or wearing more of what you already own. Your goal shapes your choices later. If you want faster mornings, for example, you will be stricter about pieces you never reach for.

Quick tidy or full reset?

A quick tidy (refolding, rehanging, removing obvious donations) can take under an hour. A full reset, where every item comes out, is better for a closet that feels overwhelming, and it usually needs a free half day. If you can't spare that, work one section at a time, such as shelves on Saturday and hanging clothes on Sunday.

What you need

  • Bags or boxes labeled donate, repair and out-of-season
  • A full-length mirror and good light
  • A clear floor or bed to lay things out on
  • Matching hangers, if you have them

Step 1: Take everything out (or one section at a time)

Seeing everything at once shows you duplicates, forgotten pieces and how much you actually own. If the closet is big, empty one zone at a time: all hanging tops, then bottoms, then shelves, then shoes. Once a section is empty, wipe down the shelves and rod and vacuum the floor before anything goes back in. A clean, empty space also helps you picture a better layout.

Step 2: Sort into keep, maybe, donate, repair and out-of-season

Pick up each piece and ask a few plain questions:

  • Does it fit now? Not "it might fit someday", but how it fits today.
  • Is it comfortable? If you keep adjusting it, you probably won't wear it.
  • Is it in good condition? Look for pilling, stretched necklines, stains, loose hems and missing buttons.
  • Do I have somewhere to wear it? A great jacket doesn't help if your life has no place for it.
  • Would I choose it again today? This question settles most borderline cases.

The try-on test for borderline pieces

If you can't decide, try the piece on in front of a mirror in good light, with the shoes you'd normally wear. Check whether it sits well on the shoulders, whether the length is where you want it, and whether the color looks good near your face. If you need a better understanding of which shades suit you, our guide to finding your skin tone depth and undertone can help.

Handle the "maybe" pile with a date

Put maybes in a box and write a review date on it, about three months out. If you haven't taken anything out of the box by then, donate it. This keeps you from getting stuck while sparing you the pressure of deciding on the spot.

Sentimental and "someday" clothes

You don't have to get rid of these, but they shouldn't take up prime hanging space. Give them one box or one shelf, kept apart from the clothes you wear every week.

Get donations and repairs out of the house

Put the donation bag in your car or by the door the same day. For repairs, set a deadline, for instance two weeks. Anything not mended by then goes to donation.

Step 3: Group what you're keeping

Start with category: tops, bottoms, dresses, outerwear, and so on. Within each category, sort by whatever fits how you dress:

  • Color: works well if you pick outfits by color. Go light to dark within each group.
  • Sleeve length or garment length: short sleeves before long sleeves, or shorter skirts before longer ones. This makes layering choices easier.
  • Occasion: if your life splits cleanly into work, casual, workout and event clothes, give each its own zone.

Category first, then color is the simplest default. Add the occasion split only if you really do dress in separate modes.

Step 4: Choose storage that suits your clothes and your space

Hang or fold?

Usually hang:

  • Blazers and coats
  • Dress shirts
  • Dresses
  • Trousers, especially if you want to keep a crease

Usually fold:

  • Knitwear and sweaters (hanging can stretch the shoulders)
  • T-shirts
  • Jeans
  • Workout clothes

Treat this as general guidance. Check care labels, and adjust for how much rod and shelf space you have.

Don't overcrowd

If you have to push hangers apart to see a garment, the rod is too full. Matching hangers keep the line tidy and make it easier to scan what you own. Leave a hand's width of room so clothes don't wrinkle against each other.

Shelves, drawers and bins

Fold knits and tees into stacks you can see from the side, so you don't need to dig. Use bins for like items (belts, scarves, gym gear), and use the vertical space above the rod for out-of-season or occasion items. Keep like with like, so there's always one obvious place for each thing.

Shoes, bags, belts, scarves and jewelry

  • Put everyday shoes at floor level or on a low rack, and rarely worn pairs higher up.
  • Hang belts and scarves on hooks or a slim hanger so you can see them all.
  • Stand bags upright (stuffed lightly so they hold their shape) rather than piling them.
  • Use a shallow tray or divided drawer for jewelry so pieces don't tangle.

Small or shared closets

In a small closet, use double-hang rods for shorter items like shirts and skirts, and move off-season clothes under the bed or on a top shelf. In a shared closet, divide it by side or by shelf, and keep a small overflow zone so neither person's clothes spill into the other's space.

Step 5: Place things by how often you wear them

Keep everyday pieces between shoulder and knee height, where you can reach them without bending or stretching. Move the rarely worn pieces higher or lower. This one rule makes a closet feel much easier to use.

Seasonal rotation

To organize clothes by season, store the pieces you won't need for a few months in labeled bins or garment bags. Clean everything before storing it. Swap at the change of season, and use the swap as your chance to reassess what you didn't wear last time. Leave transitional layers, like a light jacket or a cardigan, in the main closet all year.

Formalwear and occasion pieces

Suits, gowns and formal shoes should live together at one end of the rod, in breathable garment bags if possible, so they stay in good shape and are easy to find when needed.

Step 6: Turn a tidy closet into outfits you'll wear

An organized closet only pays off if it helps you get dressed. Spend ten minutes building three to five outfits from what you kept, and notice which pieces appear again and again.

Use simple outfit formulas

  • Smart casual: navy blazer + white tee + straight-leg jeans + white sneakers.
  • Relaxed layers: olive overshirt + cream tee + dark trousers + brown boots.
  • Balanced proportions: wide-leg trousers + fitted top, or an oversized sweater + slim trousers. Pairing loose with fitted usually works better than loose with loose, though an all-oversized look can be a deliberate choice.

Pairings that tend to work: camel with navy, charcoal with burgundy, cream with olive, and black with white or gray. Keeping a few neutrals as your base makes everything easier to mix.

Spot gaps before buying anything

If you keep building outfits that need a neutral layer, a versatile shoe, or a missing color, write it down. That list is far more useful than shopping without a plan, and it stops you from adding more things you won't wear.

A simple capsule approach

A capsule wardrobe closet is just a core of mix-and-match pieces in colors that work together. Choose two or three neutrals plus one or two accent colors, then check that most tops work with most bottoms. When you're unsure how to start your day, our 5-step guide to deciding what to wear today pairs well with a freshly organized closet.

How to keep your closet organized

  • One in, one out: when something new comes in, something leaves.
  • A 10-minute monthly reset: rehang, refold, and move anything out of place.
  • A twice-a-year review: do it at the seasonal swap and look for items you never wore.
  • Check the maybe box: on its review date, decide on everything inside it.

Where FitCheck AI can help (Android)

A physical closet still needs your hands, and no app will sort it for you. But once it's tidy, FitCheck AI can support the next step. Its digital closet and wardrobe organizer lets you organize clothes by season or occasion, save favorite and top-scoring looks, build a capsule wardrobe and plan outfits ahead for work, weekends or events.

If you're unsure about a borderline piece, you can also upload a clear, well-lit, head-to-toe photo that includes your shoes and get an AI outfit score with a breakdown of color match, proportion and balance. Treat that as a second opinion, not a professional stylist's verdict or an objective answer. The app is free on Google Play for Android, and iOS is coming soon.

faqs.answer: A quick 10-minute tidy once a month keeps things in order, and a fuller review twice a year works well alongside the seasonal swap. You only need a complete reset when the closet feels cluttered again or your lifestyle changes, such as a new job or a move.
faqs.question: How often should I reorganize my closet?

faqs.answer: Start with type (tops, bottoms, dresses, outerwear), then arrange each group by color. This gives you a logical structure and a visual flow. If your life splits clearly into work and casual, add an occasion zone on top of that.
faqs.question: Should I organize my closet by color or by type?

faqs.answer: There's no universal number. Keep what fits, is in good condition and suits the way you actually live, and what you'd happily wear this month. If you can see and reach everything without cramming, you're probably in a good range.
faqs.question: How many clothes should I keep?

faqs.answer: Use stackable bins or a freestanding shelf unit on the floor, hanging organizers on the rod for folded items, and over-the-door hooks for bags and belts. Double-hanging rods can also help you use the vertical space.
faqs.question: What's the best way to organize a closet with no shelves?

faqs.answer: Follow a one-in, one-out rule, give every category a clear home, and do a short monthly reset. Messes usually come back when there's no obvious place for something, so adjust the layout if the same spot keeps filling up.
faqs.question: How do I stop my closet getting messy again?

try-hairstyles-on-your-face.body_html:
To try hairstyles on your face, take a clear, front-facing photo and preview styles on it. You can use an AI tool that generates a new hairstyle on your picture, or compare reference photos with your own. A preview is not a promise, because your real hair texture, density and growth patterns decide the final result. It is still an inexpensive way to rule styles in or out before anyone picks up the scissors.

Why previewing a hairstyle is worth doing before you cut

A shirt that doesn't work goes back in the closet, but a cut that misses can take months to grow out. Seeing a style on your own face, rather than on a model with different features, helps you notice things a reference photo can't show. Examples are how a fringe sits against your forehead or whether a jaw-length bob suits your jawline.

What a preview can and can't tell you

A preview is good for judging overall shape and proportion: length, where the hair ends, how much volume sits around the face, and whether a fringe or side part looks balanced on you. It is not good at predicting how your hair behaves. It can't know if your hair is fine, if you have a cowlick at the front hairline, or if your curls shrink when dry. Treat it as a visual sketch, not a blueprint.

Why a good photo matters more than the tool

Whatever you use, the input shapes the output. A dim, tilted, filtered selfie makes it hard to judge anything fairly. A clear, even, straight-on photo gives you something you can assess properly. That is why the photo steps come before any tool.

How to take a photo that gives a realistic preview

Natural light and eye-level camera

Face a window so daylight falls evenly on your face. Avoid overhead lighting or a window behind you, which creates shadows and a dark outline around your hair. Hold the camera at eye level. Shooting from below exaggerates the jaw and chin, and shooting from above makes the forehead look larger. Both change how a hairstyle appears to fit.

Skip filters and heavy edits

Beauty filters smooth and reshape your face, so any hairstyle is then judged against a face that isn't quite yours. Turn them off, including any "touch up" setting in your camera app.

Neutral expression, hair pulled back or flat, face fully visible

Keep a relaxed expression and make sure your forehead, ears, jawline and neck are visible. If your hair is long or covers your face, pull it back or flatten it so your actual head shape shows. Take off hats, and consider removing glasses for your first round so you see the hair without distractions.

Take a front shot and a slight angle

A straight-on photo shows symmetry and fringe. A shot turned slightly to the side shows how layers, volume and length look in profile, which is closer to how people see you day to day. Having both lets you check each style from two views.

Ways to try hairstyles on your face

Using an app that generates AI images from your photo

With this kind of app, you provide your photo and it generates an image of you with a new hairstyle. That lets you look at a bob, curtain bangs or a pixie on your own features before deciding whether to pursue it. Remember that the image is a visual idea, not a forecast of how the cut will fall on your hair.

Using reference photos and holding them next to your own

Collect three to five photos of the cut you like, ideally from people with a similar hair type, and view them next to your own photo. Look at hair density and texture in the reference, not just the shape. A blunt bob on thick, straight hair behaves very differently on fine, wavy hair.

Low-tech options: styling, clips, wigs or temporary tweaks

You can imitate some changes at home, though only roughly. Pin long hair up to get a loose sense of a shorter length, or sweep your hair into a different parting. Clip-in fringes and inexpensive wigs can give a feel for a new fringe or length, but fit and texture won't match a real cut.

How to try hairstyles on your face with FitCheck AI

Upload or take a clear photo

If you're on Android, FitCheck AI lets you try different hairstyles on your own face. The app generates AI images of you with a new hairstyle from your photo. For hair photos, the app's own tips are to face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters. The other steps above, such as a neutral expression, hair pulled back and two angles, are general good practice rather than app requirements.

Generate a new hairstyle on your own face

Start with your clearest front photo and look at the generated image with the questions in the next section. Then compare it with the other styles you're considering, so you have more than one idea to weigh up.

Explore hairstyle, curl and hair color inspiration

The app also offers hairstyle, curl and hair color inspiration, and a way to check how a look comes together. Use it to collect ideas, such as a curl pattern you'd like to try or a shade to show a colorist. The app is free on Google Play, and you can read more about how it works.

Use the result as a second opinion, not a verdict

The result is an AI-generated image and an AI second opinion. It is not a verdict or professional stylist advice, so use it to narrow down options and start a conversation with your hairdresser.

How to judge a preview honestly

Check length, fringe and parting against your features

Ask specific questions instead of "do I like it?":

  • Length: Where does the hair end relative to your jaw, shoulders or collarbone? A chin-length cut puts the focus near the jawline, while longer lengths draw the eye further down.
  • Fringe: Does it frame your eyes or sit heavily on them? Curtain bangs are generally more forgiving than a blunt, full fringe.
  • Parting: A center part emphasizes symmetry, and a side part adds softness and lift at the crown.

Consider your real hair texture, density and curl pattern

This is where previews are weakest. Thick hair can feel heavy in a one-length cut and often benefits from layers or texturizing done by a stylist. Curly hair shrinks when it dries, so a length that looks right in the preview may sit much higher on you. Straight hair holds sharp lines well, but a heavily layered look may need daily styling to get the volume shown. If your hair is fine, ask your stylist which lengths and cutting styles keep it looking full.

Compare several options side by side

Don't pick the most dramatic result by default. Put four or five previews side by side, for example in your phone's photo gallery. Rate each on how flattering it looks, how close it is to your natural hair, and how realistic it is for your lifestyle. The ones that do well on all three are the real contenders.

Think about daily styling time and maintenance

Sharp, short or blunt cuts usually need regular trims to keep their shape. Long layers are often lower maintenance, but textured hair may still need product. If you only have a few minutes each morning, a style that depends on blow-drying and a flat iron may not last long.

Face shape as a loose starting point

Common shapes and what styles tend to balance them

Face-shape advice is a useful starting point, not a rule. The general idea is to balance the widest and narrowest areas of your face.

Face shapeTypical featuresStyles often suggested
OvalLength slightly more than width, softly rounded jawMost styles work; choose by hair type and preference
RoundSimilar width and length, soft jawLong layers, side parts, volume at the crown
SquareStrong, angular jaw and a broad foreheadSoft waves, layers that fall past the jaw, side-swept fringe
HeartWider forehead, narrower chinChin-length bobs, volume in the lower half, curtain bangs
Long / oblongLength clearly more than widthFringe, face-framing layers, width at the sides
DiamondProminent cheekbones, narrower forehead and jawFringe, styles with fullness at the chin and forehead

Why proportions, hairline and features matter as much as shape

Two people with the same face shape can suit different cuts. Your forehead height and hairline affect how a fringe sits. Your neck length affects which lengths feel balanced, and features such as a prominent nose or large eyes influence which fringes and partings look right on you.

When to ignore the rules

If you love a cut that the "rules" say you shouldn't have, look at it in a preview and judge it for yourself. Styling, confidence and the way you wear the hair often matter more than the textbook match.

Turning a preview into a hairdresser brief

Describe length, layers, fringe and finish in plain words

Hairdressers work from specifics. Instead of "something like this but nicer," say something like: "Jaw-length, one length at the back, with soft face-framing layers at the front, a long side-swept fringe, and a natural, slightly tousled finish." Mention the parting and how much styling you are willing to do.

Bring two or three reference images, including the preview

Show your preview along with a couple of photos of the cut on real people with hair similar to yours. The preview shows how the style relates to your face, and the reference photos show how the cut is built and how it moves.

Ask what is realistic for your hair type

Ask directly: "Will this work with my texture and density?" and "How much of my morning routine will it change?" A good stylist will tell you what to adjust, such as a few more layers, a longer length or a different fringe, so the result suits your hair rather than only the picture.

Don't forget color, glasses and outfit balance

How hair color interacts with skin tone and clothing colors

Color changes the whole look, so think about it as its own decision, separate from the cut. As loose guidance, many people find warm shades such as copper, caramel and golden brown flatter warmer skin tones, and cooler shades such as ash browns suit cooler ones. Strong contrast between hair and skin looks bold, and shades closer to your natural color look more subtle. Whether a color works with the clothes you wear most is personal, so pick shades you like and then hold them up against your usual wardrobe colors. A colorist can advise on what is achievable from your starting shade.

Hairstyles with glasses, necklines and your usual aesthetic

Glasses and hair compete for attention around the face. A heavy fringe can cover the top edge of thick frames, while curtain bangs usually sit comfortably around them. Necklines matter too: a short cut or an updo shows off a V-neck or open collar, while longer layers can soften a crew neck or high collar. If your wardrobe leans minimal or polished, a sleek cut tends to fit it, and a relaxed, textured cut suits casual, layered looks. For the outfit side, FitCheck AI's outfit photo check looks at color match, proportion and overall balance, which you can use as a second opinion on your clothes.

Low-risk ways to ease into a big change

Start with a trim or added layers

If a preview of a significant change excites you but you're unsure, move toward it in steps. Ask for a few inches off or some face-framing layers first, then reassess after a few weeks. It's far easier to go shorter later than to regrow.

Test a new parting or styling method for a week

Switch your parting, try a different blow-dry direction or wear your hair half-up for a week. Notice how it feels each day. If you like the preview but find the styling annoying, that tells you something useful.

Plan the in-between stage if you are growing out or going shorter

Any change has an awkward phase. When growing out a fringe, clips or headbands can help you cope. When going shorter, consider booking a shaping trim a few weeks later to keep the cut looking intentional. Knowing this in advance makes it much easier to stick with a change you wanted.

what-is-my-skin-tone.body_html:
Your skin tone has two parts: depth (how light or deep your skin looks) and undertone (the cool, warm, neutral or olive cast beneath the surface). To work out yours, look at your bare face in natural daylight, name the depth first, then use a few simple checks (veins, jewelry, a white top) to narrow down the undertone. Treat the answer as a starting point for choosing clothes, makeup and hair color, not as a rule.

Skin tone vs. undertone: two different things

Many guides use "skin tone" to mean everything at once, which is why the advice gets confusing. It helps to split it in two.

Depth: how light or deep your skin looks

Depth is the easy part. It describes how light or dark your skin appears overall, usually in loose terms like fair, light, medium, tan or deep. Depth mostly affects how much contrast you can wear. Someone with deep skin and dark hair can often carry very bright or very pale colors, while someone with fair skin and light hair may find very dark shades heavy near the face.

Undertone: the cool, warm, neutral or olive cast beneath the surface

Undertone is the subtle hue under the surface color. Two people with the same depth can have different undertones, which is why the same foundation or lipstick can look right on one and off on the other.

  • Cool: a pink, rosy or bluish cast.
  • Warm: a yellow, peachy or golden cast.
  • Neutral: a balance of the two, with no clear lean either way.
  • Olive: a muted green-gold cast, often described as sitting between warm and neutral.

Why surface color changes but undertone usually stays consistent

Your surface color shifts with sun, season and even a flush after a workout. Undertone is the steadier background hue, which makes it a useful reference for fine-tuning shades once you have considered depth and contrast. It is still a judgment call by eye, which is why the checks below work best when you combine them.

Set up first: how to look at your skin properly

Most wrong answers come from bad viewing conditions, not bad tests. Spend two minutes on setup before you try anything.

Natural daylight, bare face, no filters

Stand by a window in daylight, ideally not in direct harsh sun. Remove makeup, tinted moisturizer and self-tanner if you can. Turn off camera filters and beauty modes, since they smooth and shift color. Warm bulbs add yellow and cool LEDs add blue, so skip indoor lighting for this.

Which areas to check (jawline, neck, inner arm) and why

Check a few spots rather than one. The jawline and neck are useful comparison points next to your cheeks, but necks are often sun-exposed too, so if your neck looks clearly darker or redder than the rest of your face, don't treat it as your baseline. The inner forearm is often more sheltered from sun than the backs of your hands, though this varies from person to person. If the spots look broadly similar in cast, that is a helpful sign.

Why tanning, redness and indoor lighting can mislead you

A recent tan can make you look warmer and deeper than your usual baseline. Temporary flushing from heat, exercise or a hot shower can make skin look pinker, which may push you toward guessing "cool." If either applies, check the more sheltered areas, or repeat your checks in a few days.

How to find your undertone at home

None of these tests is proof on its own. Run all three, note which way each leans, and look for the overall pattern.

The vein check: what it can and can't tell you

Look at the veins on the inside of your wrist in daylight. Veins that look more blue or purple often point cool, and veins that look more green often point warm. If you cannot tell, or see a mix, that can suggest neutral. This check is limited: depth, lighting and how visible your veins are all change what you see, so treat it as one clue.

The jewelry check: silver vs. gold

Hold a silver piece and a gold piece against your bare skin. If silver looks crisper and more flattering, that leans cool. If gold looks richer and warmer on you, that leans warm. If both look fine, you may be neutral. This is also about personal preference, since many people love the metal their undertone "doesn't" favor.

The white paper or white top check

Hold a plain white sheet of paper or a bright white top under your chin, then compare it with an off-white or cream one. Pure white may bring out pink in cooler undertones, while cream can look more harmonious on warmer ones. Pay attention to whether your face looks fresh or slightly washed out, not just to the color of your skin.

What 'neutral' and 'olive' mean, and why they're easy to mix up

Neutral means no strong lean; both warm and cool shades may work for you. Olive has a distinct muted green-gold cast, so it can look "off" in very pink or very orange shades but lovely in earthy tones. People often mistake olive for warm because of the yellow in it, but its greenish note makes some golden shades look sallow while others look rich. Try a few options side by side to see what feels right.

CheckLeans coolLeans warmMay be neutral or olive
Wrist veinsBlue or purpleGreenA mix, or hard to tell
JewelrySilver looks betterGold looks betterBoth work
White vs. cream topBright white looks freshCream looks softerBoth fine; or muted tones suit best

How to name your depth

Fair, light, medium, tan, deep: loose descriptions, not strict categories

Compare yourself to the people around you in the same daylight and pick the word that fits best: fair, light, medium, tan or deep. Brands and charts use different names and different numbers of steps, so your label in one place may not match another. That is normal. If you want a more structured vocabulary, the Monk Skin Tone Scale is one widely used 10-shade reference for depth. It is a depth reference, so you still need the undertone checks above.

Why a skin tone chart is a rough reference, not a verdict

A skin tone chart can give you a vocabulary, but screens display color differently, and no chart can account for the full range of human skin. Use it to get close, then rely on how colors look on you in person. Your final answer might be something like "medium depth, warm undertone" or "deep, neutral-cool," and that is plenty of detail to work with.

What to do with your skin tone and undertone

Clothing colors: working with contrast, neutrals and brights

Start with contrast level (your depth, plus how your hair and eyes compare to your skin), then adjust for undertone.

  • Warm undertones often look good in camel, olive green, rust, cream, warm red and mustard. Example: a cream knit, camel trousers and a rust scarf.
  • Cool undertones often look good in navy, charcoal, emerald, cool pink, plum and true white. Example: a navy blazer, white tee and gray trousers, with an emerald top for a bolder look.
  • Neutral undertones usually have the most flexibility, so try both sides and pick by mood.
  • Olive undertones often suit earthy and jewel shades like forest green, burgundy, terracotta and warm taupe. Try them next to your face before committing to very pastel or neon options.

Colors worn near your face matter most, so test a top or scarf at the neckline. For lower-body pieces, wear whatever you like. If you want to see how colors work together in a full outfit, Live FitCheck can check an outfit live with the camera and give color analysis, matching and styling suggestions. Treat those suggestions as one opinion to weigh, not a final verdict.

Makeup: testing foundation on the jawline in daylight

To find a foundation shade, swatch two or three close options along the jawline, not the back of your hand, and check them in daylight. The right one tends to blend into your neck without a visible line. Then consider undertone: a shade that looks slightly gray on you may be too cool, and one that looks yellow or orange may be too warm. For blush and lip, warm undertones often like peach, coral and terracotta, while cool undertones often like rose, berry and cool pink. Neutral and olive skin can usually go either way, so try both. To preview a lip color before you buy it, FitCheck AI's live virtual makeup try-on lets you see looks such as lipstick on your own face through the live camera.

Hair color and jewelry metals: general starting points

Warm undertones often pair well with golden blonde, honey, copper and warm brown, plus gold jewelry. Cool undertones often pair well with ash tones, espresso, blue-black and silver jewelry. Neutral skin can wear mixed metals easily. These are widely used starting points, not requirements. If you are weighing a bigger change, previewing it first helps; our guide on trying hairstyles on your face before you commit to a cut covers how.

When to break the rules: taste, occasion and personality

Undertone guidance is a shortcut for finding colors that flatter you, but it will not tell you what you enjoy wearing. A color that is "wrong" for your undertone can still work if you keep it away from your face, add a scarf or necklace in a better shade, or simply love it. Occasion matters too: a uniform, a wedding palette or a dress code often outranks any color rule.

Where a camera-based tool fits in

What FitCheck's live skin analysis does

FitCheck AI's live skin analysis uses the camera to give an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. It is not a skin tone or undertone test, so keep using the daylight checks above to work out your depth and undertone. If you are curious about cosmetic suggestions for your look, you can weigh them alongside what you see yourself. The app is available on Android (free on Google Play), and an iOS version is coming soon.

Photo tips: natural light, eye level, no filters

For makeup and beauty features, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and turn off any filters.

Why AI feedback is a starting point, not a professional color analysis

AI feedback is an opinion, not a measurement, and it is not a professional stylist or a formal color analysis. Use it as one input alongside your own checks and your own sense of what looks and feels like you.

Not medical advice

This guide is about cosmetic style only

Everything here is about color, makeup and style choices. It does not diagnose, detect or treat anything about your skin, and it cannot tell you anything about skin health.

See a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern or change

AI feedback, including from skin analysis tools, is not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern or change you notice.

faqs.answer: Your surface color can shift with the seasons, sun exposure and the way your skin looks day to day, so your depth may look lighter or deeper at different times. Undertone is generally steadier, though perception can change with a tan or temporary flush. If you are unsure, re-check in daylight on a sheltered area like your inner arm.
faqs.question: Can my skin tone change over time?

faqs.answer: That is common, because warm bulbs, cool LEDs and filters all push color around. Trust natural daylight over indoor lighting, and repeat your checks at a window at a different time of day. If results still conflict, you may simply be neutral, and a flexible color palette will serve you well.
faqs.question: What if my results are different in different lights?

faqs.answer: This often points to a neutral undertone, which gives you the most room to experiment. Pick colors by what you like and the mood you want, and test them at the neckline. You can also lean on contrast and depth, which often matter as much as undertone.
faqs.question: What if I seem to fit both warm and cool?

faqs.answer: No. Undertone is a helpful shortcut, not a requirement. If you love a shade that isn't the textbook match, wear it away from your face, pair it with a flattering color near your neckline, or just enjoy it.

what-makeup-suits-my-face.body_html:
The makeup that suits your face comes from a combination of undertone, natural contrast, feature placement, and the finish you like, not from face shape alone. Answer the six questions below, jot down your results, and you will end up with a simple makeup profile: a shade family, a level of definition, and a placement plan you can test at home.

Here is the quiz at a glance, so you know what to expect before you start:

QuestionWhat you decideWhat it guides
1. UndertoneWarm, cool or neutralBlush, lip and eyeshadow shade families
2. ContrastLow, medium or highHow defined or soft the look is
3. Face shapeRound, oval, square, heart or longBlush, bronzer and highlighter placement
4. EyesEye color and eye shapeEyeshadow, liner and mascara choices
5. LipsShade and texture you likeLip color and finish
6. Finish and timeDewy, natural or matte; 5, 15 or full-glam minutesYour routine and occasion looks

How this 'what makeup suits my face' quiz works

What suits you is more than face shape

Many makeup quizzes only ask about face shape, or only about skin tone. Each is a piece of the picture. Undertone and contrast guide color. Face shape and eye shape guide placement. Finish and time guide how the look feels on you day to day. This quiz covers all of them.

How to use the quiz

Write your answer to each question as you go: undertone, contrast level, face shape, eye color and shape, lip preference, finish and time. There is nothing to submit and no score. It is a self-guided checklist in this article.

What you'll end up with

Your result will read something like: warm undertone, medium contrast, oval face, soft-glam everyday look. Then you will turn that into specific products and positions.

Before you start: set up so your answers are accurate

Natural light, clean face, mirror at eye level

Sit facing a window in daylight, with a bare or lightly moisturized face and your mirror at eye level. Overhead bathroom bulbs and yellow lamps can change how skin and hair look.

Skip filters and heavy color-correcting lighting

Beauty filters, ring lights, and strongly tinted lamps can shift your apparent undertone. If you are using photos, take them unfiltered.

Question 1: What is your undertone?

Quick checks

These are informal checks, not proof, so treat each one as a hint.

  • Veins: mostly green may suggest warm, mostly blue or purple may suggest cool, and a mix may suggest neutral.
  • Jewelry: if gold looks richer on you, you may lean warm. If silver does, you may lean cool. If both work, you may be neutral.
  • White vs. cream: stark white may flatter cooler undertones, while ivory and cream may flatter warmer ones.

None of these is definitive, so look for the answer that shows up most often. Our guide to finding your skin tone depth and undertone goes deeper if you are unsure.

What each undertone means for shades

  • Warm: peach or coral blush, golden bronzer, terracotta or brick lips, bronze and copper eyeshadow often work well.
  • Cool: rose or berry blush, soft pink or raspberry lips, taupe, plum, and silver-toned shadows often work well.
  • Neutral: you can borrow from both. Dusty rose, mauve, and true red are reliable starting points.

Question 2: How strong is your natural contrast?

Compare skin, hair, and eyes

Look at how different the depth is between your skin, hair, and eyes. Dark hair with fair skin and light eyes is high contrast. Dark hair, tan skin, and dark eyes, or light hair with light skin and light eyes, is usually lower contrast. Most people land in the middle.

What each level suggests

  • High contrast: you can often carry defined looks well, such as a clear lip, a crisp liner, or deeper shadow.
  • Medium contrast: flexible. Pick one focal point, either eyes or lips, and keep the rest softer.
  • Low contrast: tonal, blended looks tend to feel natural. Think a soft brown liner, a sheer wash of blush, and a lip close to your natural color.

Soft-focus vs. defined

These are tendencies, not rules. If you love a bold lip with low contrast coloring, wear it. Just expect it to read as a statement rather than blend in.

Question 3: What is your face shape, and where does color go?

Face shape as a loose starting point

Pull your hair back and look straight on. Is your face about as wide as it is long (round), longer than it is wide (long), angular at the jaw (square), wider at the forehead than the chin (heart), or gently balanced (oval)? Many people are a blend, so choose the closest.

Blush, bronzer, and highlighter placement ideas

  • Round: sweep blush slightly up and back toward the temples, and keep bronzer light just under the cheekbone.
  • Oval: most placements work. Try blush on the apples blending toward the temples.
  • Square: blend blush on the apples in a soft, rounded shape, and use a little bronzer at the corners of the jaw to soften.
  • Heart: place blush at the apples and a touch of bronzer at the temples and chin to balance.
  • Long: sweep blush more horizontally across the cheeks rather than high on the cheekbone, which adds width.

Highlighter usually goes on the high points of the cheekbones, with a small amount down the nose bridge if you like.

When to ignore face-shape rules

If a placement makes you feel good in the mirror, keep it. Face-shape guidance is a shortcut for balance, not a requirement.

Question 4: What eye color and eye shape are you working with?

Shades that tend to bring out each eye color

  • Blue: warm bronze, copper, and peach.
  • Green: plum, burgundy, and warm brown.
  • Hazel: olive green, gold, and soft purple, depending on which tone you want to emphasize.
  • Brown: very flexible. Try emerald, teal, navy, bronze, or soft berry for contrast.

Simple liner and mascara placement

  • Hooded: apply shadow slightly above the crease so it shows when your eyes are open, and keep liner thin.
  • Wide-set: deepen the inner corners a little.
  • Close-set: brighten the inner corner and concentrate depth on the outer half.
  • Upturned: a smudged, soft line along the lower lashes balances the lift.
  • Downturned: wing liner and mascara slightly upward and outward, and keep the outer lower lash line light.

Glasses wearers

Frames can hide shadow near the brow bone, so slightly more definition on the lid and lashes helps. Blush that sits a touch higher keeps color from disappearing under the frame.

Question 5: What lip color and finish feel like you?

Choose by undertone and contrast

Start with your undertone family from Question 1: coral and brick for warm, berry and cool rose for cool, mauve and true red for neutral. Then use contrast: high-contrast coloring can often wear deeper or brighter shades, and low-contrast coloring often looks best a shade or two from the natural lip.

Sheer, satin, matte, or gloss

This is about comfort and the look you want. Sheer tints are low-effort, satin is a middle ground, matte looks polished and defined, and gloss adds a fuller, fresher look.

Optional tweaks for fuller or thinner lips

Lighter, shinier shades can make lips look fuller. Deeper, matte shades can make them look more defined. Both are purely cosmetic choices.

Question 6: What finish do you prefer, and how much time do you have?

Dewy, natural, or matte

Treat this as a style preference. Dewy looks luminous, natural sits in between, and matte looks smooth and controlled. Pick the one you enjoy wearing.

Routines by time

  • Five minutes: tinted moisturizer or concealer where you want it, cream blush, mascara, tinted lip balm.
  • Fifteen minutes: add foundation, brow fill, a wash of eyeshadow, and a defined lip.
  • Full glam: add contour, highlighter, liner, and lashes, with a setting product where you want it to last.

Occasions

Everyday and work looks usually lean softer and more blended. Date nights and events are where you can raise the definition, either with a deeper lip or a smokier eye, but not both at full volume.

Your results: match your answers to a makeup profile

Palette cheat sheet

UndertoneBlushLipsEyes
WarmPeach, coral, warm apricotCoral, terracotta, brickBronze, copper, olive
CoolRose, pink, berryRaspberry, cool rose, plumTaupe, plum, slate
NeutralDusty rose, soft peachMauve, true redSoft brown, mauve, champagne

Contrast: how defined to make the look

High contrast: pick a clear focal point. Medium: one focal point, the rest soft. Low: blend everything and stay tonal.

Three sample profiles

  1. Warm, medium contrast, soft everyday glow: a light base, peach cream blush on the apples, a bronze wash on the lids, brown mascara, and a coral satin lip.
  2. Cool, high contrast, defined evening look: a satin base, rose blush, taupe shadow with black liner, and a berry or classic cool red lip.
  3. Neutral, low contrast, five-minute routine: tinted moisturizer, dusty rose cream blush dabbed on the cheeks, soft brown mascara, and a mauve sheer lip.

How to test your results before you commit

Swatch in daylight

Swatch foundation along your jawline and blush or lip color on the inner wrist or the back of your hand, then check them near a window. A foundation shade that seems to disappear into the skin at your jaw is often a good match, though it is worth checking in a second light.

Compare two looks in unfiltered photos

Take an unfiltered photo of each look in the same light and compare them side by side. Photos can show things the mirror does not, such as a blush that is too heavy or a lip that fades.

Change one thing at a time

Swap only the lip, the blush, or the eye, and keep the rest the same. That makes it easy to tell what is working.

Trust comfort

If a look does not feel like you, adjust it. Your quiz result is a starting point, not a rule you have to follow.

Where FitCheck AI can help you check your makeup

FitCheck AI does not have a built-in quiz. The quiz above is self-guided and lives in this article. Once you have your profile, the AI makeup assistant can give personalized suggestions and feedback on a makeup look, from an everyday glow to full glam, based on your appearance. The app also has live virtual makeup try-on, so you can preview something like a lipstick shade on your own face with the live camera, plus makeup assist with live camera guidance.

For best results, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level, and avoid filters. Treat the feedback as a second opinion and a starting point. It is not perfect, not objective, and not a substitute for a professional stylist, and your own taste still has the final say.

Not medical advice

Cosmetic style guidance only

This guide, and any AI feedback, covers cosmetic style choices such as shade, placement, and finish. It is not medical advice and cannot diagnose or treat any condition.

See a professional for health concerns

If you have a concern about your skin, scalp, or hair, see a dermatologist or doctor rather than relying on makeup tips or an app.

faqs.answer: They do different jobs. Skin tone and undertone guide which shades look harmonious, while face shape only loosely guides where to place blush, bronzer, and highlighter. If you have to prioritize, start with color and treat face shape as optional fine-tuning.
faqs.question: Is face shape or skin tone more important for choosing makeup?

faqs.answer: Your undertone is generally considered stable, but your surface depth can darken or look warmer after sun exposure. That means you may need a slightly deeper foundation or bronzer in summer while your blush and lip families stay the same.
faqs.question: Can my undertone change with a tan?

faqs.answer: That is common. A neutral undertone, a mixed face shape, or medium contrast all mean you have flexibility. Pick the answer that appears most often, test two looks side by side in daylight, and go with the one that feels most like you.
faqs.question: What if my quiz answers point in different directions?

faqs.answer: Check in when something changes: a new hair color, a big seasonal change in your skin tone, or when a favorite shade stops feeling right. Otherwise, a quick daylight swatch test every few months is plenty.
faqs.question: How often should I revisit my makeup palette?

what-should-i-wear-today.body_html:
If you're wondering what to wear today, start with two facts: the weather and what your day involves. Then pick one piece you want to wear, build around it with a neutral base and one accent, and finish with shoes that suit your plans. The steps below take about five minutes, and the formulas after them cover most days.

A 5-step way to decide what to wear today

Step 1: Check the weather and your day

Look at the temperature range, rain or wind, and where you'll spend your time. A day split between a cold commute and a warm office needs different clothes than a day outdoors. Also note how much walking, sitting or carrying you'll do. Comfort limits come first, and style works within them.

Step 2: Pick your dress-up level

Think of a dial from 1 (loungewear) to 5 (formal). Errands sit around 2, most offices around 3 or 4, and a dinner out around 3 to 5 depending on the venue. You can move the dial with small swaps: sneakers down, loafers up, a blazer up, a knit down.

Step 3: Choose one anchor piece

Deciding is easier when you don't start from zero. Pick one item you want to wear, such as a favorite pair of trousers, a jacket that fits well, or a dress you haven't worn in a while. Everything else supports it.

Step 4: Build around it with color and proportion

Pair the anchor with neutrals (black, white, cream, grey, navy, denim, tan) and allow at most one accent color. If the anchor is loose or oversized, keep the other half of the outfit more fitted, and the reverse. More detail is in the color and proportion section below.

Step 5: Finish with shoes and one accessory

Shoes set the tone of the whole outfit, so choose them for both the dress-up level and the day's walking. Then add one accessory, like a belt, a watch, a scarf or a bag, and stop there.

What to wear today based on the weather

Warm days: breathable fabrics and light layers

Cotton, linen and other lightweight fabrics help you stay comfortable. Light colors reflect heat better than dark ones. A short-sleeve shirt with relaxed trousers or a simple dress works well. Keep a thin overshirt or cardigan in your bag for air-conditioned rooms.

Cool days: layering that you can add or remove

Aim for pieces that come off easily: a tee or shirt, a knit or light jacket over it, and trousers or jeans. If you warm up indoors, you can drop a layer without breaking the outfit.

Cold days: base layer, mid layer and outer layer

Use three layers: a thin base that sits close to the skin, an insulating mid layer like a sweater or fleece, and a coat to block wind. Keep the layers in similar color families (for example, grey base, charcoal knit, black coat) so the bulk looks intentional. Add a hat, scarf or gloves as needed.

Rain and wind: practical shoes and outer layers that still look put together

Choose water-resistant shoes or boots and a jacket with a hood. Avoid long hems that will drag in puddles, and consider slightly shorter or cuffed trousers. In wind, fitted layers and a closed-front jacket are more comfortable than loose, flowing pieces.

When the temperature swings during the day

Dress for the part of the day when you'll be outside the longest, then add one removable layer for the rest. A shirt plus a light jacket or cardigan covers a wide range better than a single heavy piece.

What to wear today by occasion

Office or work

Aim for a 3 or 4 on the dial. Try tailored or straight trousers with a shirt or fine knit and loafers, flats or clean leather sneakers if your workplace allows. Fit matters more than price here: sleeves and hems that sit properly make simple pieces look sharper.

Casual day out or errands

Go for a tee or sweatshirt, relaxed jeans or chinos, and comfortable sneakers. Add a light jacket or overshirt to make it look more deliberate.

Date night or dinner

Move the dial up one notch from your everyday look. A fitted knit with dark trousers and boots, or a dress with a jacket, usually works. Choose something you feel comfortable sitting in for a couple of hours.

Events, parties or a night out

Check the dress code first, then pick a statement element: a bold color, a textured fabric or standout shoes. Keep the rest quiet so the outfit doesn't compete with itself.

Workouts and active days

Choose moisture-friendly fabrics, supportive shoes for the activity and layers you can remove after warming up. If you're heading somewhere afterward, bring one cleaner top to change into.

Travel or a long day on your feet

Prioritize comfortable shoes, stretchy or relaxed bottoms and layers with pockets. Dark or mid-tone colors hide small spills and creases better than white or pale shades.

Simple outfit formulas you can reuse

Formulas save you from rethinking every outfit from scratch. Swap in colors you own and the structure holds.

FormulaExampleBest for
Tee or shirt + straight or relaxed trousers + clean sneakersWhite tee, olive trousers, white sneakersCasual days, errands, relaxed offices
Knit + tailored pants + loafers or bootsNavy knit, grey trousers, brown loafersWork, dinners, cooler weather
Dress + jacket + comfortable shoesBlack midi dress, denim or tailored jacket, sneakers or flatsDressy-casual days, events
Layered neutrals + one accent colorCream top, grey cardigan, tan trousers, rust scarfAny day you want depth without effort
Coordinated set + simple shoesMatching linen shirt and shorts, minimal sandalsWarm days, travel, quick mornings

Color and proportion basics for a quick check

Neutrals plus one accent color

Build the base from neutrals, then add one color you like. Some reliable pairings are navy with camel, olive with cream, charcoal with burgundy, and black with white plus a single pop such as cobalt. If you want to know which shades suit you most, our guide on finding your skin tone depth and undertone is a useful starting point.

Balancing fitted and loose pieces

Pair a roomy top with slimmer or straight bottoms, or a fitted top with wide-leg pants. When both halves are very loose, the outfit can look shapeless, which is fine if it's intentional, but tucking in or adding a belt gives it structure.

Matching metals, shoe tones and bag or belt tones loosely

Your belt, shoes and bag don't need to match exactly, but staying in the same family (brown with tan, black with grey) looks cohesive. Similarly, try to stick with one metal tone for jewelry, watch and buckles on most days.

Mixing patterns carefully

Mix patterns of different scales, such as a thin stripe with a larger check, and keep them in a shared color. If that feels risky, wear one pattern and keep everything else solid.

What to do when you feel like you have nothing to wear

Look for the real problem: fit, comfort, occasion or boredom

A full closet and "nothing to wear" usually means something specific: items that don't fit well, clothes that are uncomfortable, no pieces for a certain occasion, or just fatigue with the same combinations. Name the problem and the fix gets clearer.

Re-style pieces you already own in new combinations

Try an old shirt as a light jacket, a dress over trousers, or a different shoe with a familiar outfit. Changing just one item, such as the shoes or the outer layer, can make a familiar look feel new.

Build a small capsule base that mixes easily

A capsule base is a handful of versatile pieces in a shared palette: a few tops, two or three bottoms, a jacket and a couple of pairs of shoes. Because everything coordinates, most combinations work.

Save outfits you liked so you can repeat them

Photograph outfits that felt good and put them somewhere you can find quickly. Repeating a good outfit is not a failure; it is a shortcut.

A 30-second check before you leave the house

  1. Comfort test: sit down, walk a few steps and reach overhead. If anything pinches, slips or rides up, change it now.
  2. Fit and balance: check a full-length mirror. Look at where hems fall, whether the shoulders sit properly and whether the proportions feel balanced.
  3. Color and shoes: make sure the colors work together and the shoes match the dress-up level and the weather.
  4. Photo check: take a quick head-to-toe photo. A photo can give you a different view than a mirror and may show a bunched layer or a clashing tone.

How FitCheck AI can help you decide what to wear

If you'd like a second opinion, FitCheck AI is a free Android app with an outfit checker, Live FitCheck, a digital closet and virtual outfit try-on. With the AI outfit check, you take or upload a clear, well-lit, head-to-toe photo including your shoes and get an AI outfit score plus a breakdown of color match, proportion and overall balance, with ideas such as switching shoes or adjusting color contrast. Outfit scoring photos are processed on your device. Live FitCheck lets you check an outfit live with your camera, with an outfit rating, color analysis, matching and styling suggestions.

For the longer-term habit, the digital closet lets you save top-scoring looks, organize clothes by season or occasion and plan outfits ahead for work, workouts, date nights and casual weekends. Virtual outfit try-on creates AI-generated images of you in different outfits from your photo; these are previews, not a guide to exact garment fit or sizing.

Keep in mind that a score is an AI opinion. It is a starting point, not an objective verdict, and not a replacement for a professional stylist. Your comfort, the dress code and your own taste still make the final call.

faqs.answer: Pick comfortable pieces you like and make them look intentional with one upgrade, such as a clean pair of shoes, a well-fitting jacket or a favorite accessory. A tee, relaxed jeans or chinos and sneakers is a dependable base. Check the weather and add a layer in case you end up going out.
faqs.question: What should I wear today if I have no plans?

faqs.answer: Dress for the conditions you'll be exposed to the longest, then add one layer that is easy to remove or carry, like a cardigan, overshirt or light jacket. Choose shoes that handle the worst part of the forecast, such as rain. A small bag or a jacket with pockets makes carrying a layer easier.
faqs.question: How do I dress for changing weather?

faqs.answer: Use an outfit formula and start from one anchor piece, then add neutrals and a single accent. Deciding the night before cuts the morning rush further. Having a few go-to combinations also helps on days when you're short on time.
faqs.question: How do I pick an outfit quickly in the morning?

faqs.answer: Yes. Check the forecast and your calendar, then choose an outfit for each day and note which ones can be adapted if the weather changes. You can do this with photos on your phone or with the outfit planning tools in a digital closet app. Planning ahead helps most with busy mornings and repeat occasions like work.
faqs.question: Can I plan my outfits for the week?

faqs.answer: No. A score is an AI opinion that can point out things like color match or balance, but it isn't objective and doesn't replace a professional stylist. Treat it as a second opinion and weigh it against comfort, fit, the occasion and what you like wearing.
faqs.question: Is an AI outfit score the final word on my outfit?
